findings.paper_title: 10. Performance1_ Report Q1 26-27 (EM)
findings.headline: Pothole and road edge repairs completed within 28-day target improved to 93.3%, up from 88.9% in the prior quarter and now tracking toward the 95% target by Q2.
findings.detail: This measure was Red for all of 2025-26 (ranging 76.8%-89.2%) and is now Amber with clear upward trajectory. Council is working closely with contractor to identify and rectify shortcomings. Clear operational improvement trend in a core highway maintenance service.
findings.matters: Highway maintenance is core asset management. Sustained underperformance can spiral defect damage, create liability exposure, and damage reputation. The improving trend demonstrates the council can fix operational performance problems through contractor engagement.
findings.figures: 93.3% (Q1 26-27) vs 95% target; up from 88.9% (Q4 25-26); Red throughout 2025-26 range 76.8%-89.2%.
findings.quote: This is a clear improvement from 2025/26 Q4 and on full year figures for 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance1_ Report Q1 26-27 (EM)
findings.headline: Household waste recycling rate fell to 52.7%, below the 57% target and down from 54.5% in the previous quarter.
findings.detail: Decline attributed to contractor sending wood waste for recovery rather than recycling due to weak recycled material markets. Extreme heat in June reduced garden waste tonnages. Contractor's year-end forecast 55.7%, still below target. Q1 data provisional and subject to DEFRA validation.
findings.matters: Recycling rate is both an environmental performance metric and a potential contractual/cost issue. Declines can trigger contract performance queries and suggest external market and weather pressures on waste contractor performance.
findings.figures: 52.7% (Q1) vs 57% target; down from 54.5% (Q4 25-26); contractor forecast 55.7% year-end.
findings.quote: Wider industry challenges have meant our contractor has had to send wood for recovery and not recycling which has led to a fall in recycling rate, however, they are hoping that the market for recycled wood will pick up from July onwards.

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance1_ Report Q1 26-27 (EM)
findings.headline: Staff turnover remained at 15.0% against target of 13%, with the council stating the figure 'is likely to remain higher than the target given the continued restructure proposals the council continues to undertake.'
findings.detail: Turnover consistently above target throughout the year. Top three reasons for resignation: career development, relocation, health reasons. Vacancy rate 15.5% (down from 17.9%). Council signals structural nature of problem: ongoing reorganisations will sustain elevated turnover. This creates dual pressure—ongoing recruitment costs and sustained service delivery disruption.
findings.matters: Persistent above-target staff turnover indicates difficulty retaining staff, creating direct costs (recruitment, training, lost knowledge) and indirect costs (service disruption, quality degradation). Council's own statement that restructures will keep turnover elevated signals loss of institutional capacity.
findings.figures: 15.0% outturn vs 13% target (Q1); 15.5% vacancy rate vs 17.9% previous quarter; consistently above target throughout year.
findings.quote: However, it is likely that the figure will remain higher than the target given the continued restructure proposals the council continues to undertake.

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance1_ Report Q1 26-27 (EM)
findings.headline: Rough sleeping increased to 13 people on a single night (target 6) and long-term entrenched homelessness rose to 10 (target 3), with affordable housing completions at 24 against target of 37.
findings.detail: Both rough-sleeping measures are new for 2026-27. Council attributes increase partly to warmer months but notes 'those who are entrenched in homelessness has increased.' Housing completion pipeline delayed, with registered provider completions typically Q4 due to construction practices. Housing shortage is stated reason for failure to meet relief duty (50.9% secured 6+ months accommodation vs 55% target) and is driving the rough-sleeper cohort.
findings.matters: Rising homelessness and entrenched rough sleeping indicate unmet housing need and growing demand on council services requiring sustained expenditure. Housing shortage constrains the council's ability to discharge statutory homelessness relief duty, increasing pressure on temporary accommodation services.
findings.figures: 13 rough sleepers vs target 6; 10 long-term rough sleepers vs target 3; 24 affordable homes completed vs 37 target; 50.9% relief duty success vs 55% target.
findings.quote: Those who are entrenched in homelessness has increased.

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance1_ Report Q1 26-27 (EM)
findings.headline: Safeguarding outcomes in adult protection declined, with only 56.3% of Section 42 enquiries resulting in fully achieved outcomes, compared to 68% target.
findings.detail: Outcomes have deteriorated consistently through year (68%→61.7%→63.5%→62.7%→56.3%). Of 142 Q1 cases, only 80 achieved full outcomes, 48 achieved partial outcomes, 14 achieved none. Council has commissioned audit of unachieved cases. Trend is downward despite council noting partially achieved cases increased.
findings.matters: Declining safeguarding outcomes indicate adult protection service is under capacity or strain, creating governance risk, regulatory exposure, and reputational damage. Councils have non-discretionary duty to protect vulnerable adults.
findings.figures: 56.3% vs 68% target (Q1); 80/142 full outcomes; YTD deterioration from 68% to 56.3%.
findings.quote: Although % fully achieved has dropped, partially achieved has increased. Only 14 out of 142 cases where outcomes not achieved.

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance1_ Report Q1 26-27 (EM)
findings.headline: Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCP) issued to only 5.5% of applicants within the required 20-week statutory timeframe, compared to 60% target.
findings.detail: Only 5 of 91 plans issued in time. Severe structural constraints identified: staffing shortfall (4 FTE case officers deployed vs 10 FTE benchmark based on 543 annual assessment requests in 2025), 120-strong backlog of educational psychology assessments awaiting completion, and school consultation delays (schools can take up to 10 working days to respond). EHCP demand has grown 280% since 2020 (99 → 376), vastly outpacing staffing capacity.
findings.matters: EHCPs represent a non-discretionary legal duty; failure to assess and issue within 20 weeks exposes councils to tribunal challenge, cost awards, and reputational damage. Persistent shortfall between need and capacity creates ongoing financial and legal risk.
findings.figures: 5.5% outturn vs 60% target (Q1 26-27); 5 of 91 plans issued on time; 543 requests in 2025 vs 10 FTE benchmark; 120 EP assessment backlog; EHCP numbers up 280% since 2020.
findings.quote: In 2025 we had 543 requests, which means the benchmark would have been 10FTE Case Officers. Last year we had 4FTE. With the additional funding we have been given for this financial year, we now have 6 FTE.

findings.paper_title: 7. Appendix A - Capital Reprofiling
findings.headline: Multiple education infrastructure schemes delayed to 2027 affecting school capacity, totaling £1.3m
findings.detail: Three education capital schemes totaling £1.3m externally funded are being reprofiled to 2027: Brookfields School accessibility (£454k), Brookfields expansion for early years and Key Stage 3 (£409k), and Westwood Farm SEND provision (£393k). Brookfields School Phase 1 works are now expected to take longer than originally planned; Brookfields expansion is awaiting cost confirmation before Procurement Board submission; Westwood Farm's start has been delayed.
findings.matters: Multiple delays across education infrastructure schemes affecting school capacity signal timing pressures in the education capital programme. This affects the council's ability to deliver planned service expansion and accessibility improvements.
findings.quote: Phase 1 works are now expected to take longer than originally planned, with practical completion anticipated in summer 2027

findings.paper_title: 7. Appendix A - Capital Reprofiling
findings.headline: SEND infrastructure delivery constrained by wider SEND reform programme pressures
findings.detail: The council's Special Education Needs infrastructure scheme (£523k externally funded) is experiencing delivery delays. The reprofiling justification attributes this to external pressures. Current forecast provides for design fees and potential construction activity in 2026/27, with reprofiling requested to reflect the revised timing of planned works.
findings.matters: SEND is a statutory obligation and major demand driver. External reform programme pressures affecting infrastructure delivery signal risks to the council's ability to meet statutory SEND demand and obligations.
findings.quote: Delivery has been affected by wider SEND reform programme pressures

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance4_Appendix C - Q1 26-27 KoPIs (Key Operational) - All status'
findings.headline: 18 children's social workers carrying more than 18 cases each; improving but far above zero target
findings.detail: Q1 reports 18 social workers with caseloads exceeding 18 cases (target 0). This represents improvement from 22 in the prior quarter and 25 two quarters prior. The council notes caseloads are 'linked to many factors' and impact 'recruitment and retention,' with average caseload now 18—'a significant improvement to previous year when some were as high as 35.'
findings.matters: High social worker caseloads, even if trending down, create service quality and staffing stability risks; the council remains far from target despite showing improvement.

findings.quote: Those on high caseloads are on an average of 18. This is a significant improvement to previous year when some were as high as 35.

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance4_Appendix C - Q1 26-27 KoPIs (Key Operational) - All status'
findings.headline: Safeguarding enquiry outcomes only 56.3% fully achieved against 68% target
findings.detail: S42 safeguarding enquiries where the subject's desired outcomes were fully achieved reached only 56.3% in Q1 (80/142) against a 68% target. The council notes: 'Although % fully achieved has dropped, partially achieved (48) has increased. Only 14 out of 142 cases where outcomes not achieved.' The Safeguarding Manager is conducting an audit of those cases.
findings.matters: Below-target achievement of fully desired safeguarding outcomes, even with increased partial achievement, creates governance and audit risk that requires investigation.
findings.figures: 56.3% (80/142 Q1) vs 68% target; 48 partially achieved; 14 not achieved
findings.quote: Although % fully achieved has dropped, partially achieved (48) has increased. Only 14 out of 142 cases where outcomes not achieved.

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance4_Appendix C - Q1 26-27 KoPIs (Key Operational) - All status'
findings.headline: Housing relief duty outcomes at 50.9% against 55% target due to affordable housing shortage
findings.detail: Only 50.9% of households exiting relief duty secure accommodation for 6+ months (target 55%; Q1: 54/106). The council identifies the constraint as structural: 'Ongoing shortage of affordable housing resulting in reduced number of households being able to secure settled accommodation for at least 6 months.' The council is reviewing landlord incentives and tenancy-readiness support.
findings.matters: A structural affordable housing shortage means the council cannot meet statutory homelessness duty targets within timeframes, creating a persistent cost and demand management pressure.
findings.quote: Ongoing shortage of affordable housing resulting in reduced number of households being able to secure settled accommodation for at least 6 months.

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance4_Appendix C - Q1 26-27 KoPIs (Key Operational) - All status'
findings.headline: Single-night rough sleeper count at 13 against target of 6; long-term entrenched homeless at 10 against target of 3
findings.detail: Q1 recorded 13 rough sleepers on a single night (target 6) and 10 long-term rough sleepers (target 3). The council attributes the single-night increase to seasonal warming but signals a structural trend: 'Those who are entrenched in homelessness has increased and we will be required to review our target priority group in line with Homes England outcome matrix.'
findings.matters: Rising rough homelessness indicates either deteriorating community conditions or service capacity constraints; both create demand pressure and budget implications for councils.
findings.figures: 13 single-night vs target 6; 10 long-term vs target 3
findings.quote: Those who are entrenched in homelessness has increased and we will be required to review our target priority group in line with Homes England outcome matrix

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance4_Appendix C - Q1 26-27 KoPIs (Key Operational) - All status'
findings.headline: Council cannot report on four core children's services KPIs due to Mosaic system implementation failure
findings.detail: Performance measures tracking repeat referrals, repeat child protection plans, children in care placements, and care leaver employment are all marked unavailable. The council reports: 'Data unavailable due to the implementation of the Mosaic system and the temporary unavailability of reporting.' This creates a reporting blackout on critical safeguarding and social care metrics mid-year.
findings.matters: A major system implementation has left the council without visibility into key child safety and outcomes measures, creating audit risk and limiting monitoring capability during a period of service demand pressure.
findings.figures: Measures 10, 11, 12, 13 all marked n/a

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance4_Appendix C - Q1 26-27 KoPIs (Key Operational) - All status'
findings.headline: Staff turnover at 15% against 13% target, forecast to remain elevated due to ongoing restructuring
findings.detail: The council reports staff turnover at 15% in Q1 against a 13% target. The shortfall is attributed to restructuring activity including redundancies and voluntary departures. The council explicitly forecasts this will persist: 'it is likely that the figure will remain higher than the target given the continued restructure proposals the council continues to undertake.' Top departure reasons cited are career development, relocation, and health.
findings.matters: Sustained elevated turnover during restructuring increases recruitment costs and disrupts service delivery; finance directors need accurate forecasts of restructuring costs versus unplanned turnover.
findings.figures: 15% actual vs 13% target; Q1: 234 / 1,560
findings.quote: However, it is likely that the figure will remain higher than the target given the continued restructure proposals the council continues to undertake.

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance3_Appendix B - Q1 26-27 CSDM (Business as Usual) - All status'
findings.headline: Attendance at Culture and Library Services events fell 15% short of Q1 target, attributed partly to a vacant Marketing Manager post.
findings.detail: The council recorded 12,790 attendees against a 15,000 target, described as down compared to the same quarter in the prior year. The council attributes shortfalls to a vacant dedicated Marketing Manager post, downscaling of the museum events programme after capital funding for the damp remediation project was withdrawn, staff capacity diverted to a museum store relocation, and unplanned library closures during June 2026 extreme temperatures.
findings.matters: A vacant post directly affecting service delivery suggests staffing pressure; if cultural services underperform due to insufficient resourcing, it may impact income generation or community engagement.
findings.figures: 12,790 actual attendees vs 15,000 target; reported as down on same quarter prior year
findings.quote: For all the Culture and Libraries venues the figures are down on the same period last year - attendance at events and activities has been affected by not having a dedicated Marketing Manager in post. Museum numbers are lower than usual because of the museum store move project which meant that there has not been staff capacity to run events or organise new exhibitions.

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance3_Appendix B - Q1 26-27 CSDM (Business as Usual) - All status'
findings.headline: Three financial governance measures show no Q1 data: the Financial Improvement Plan, CIPFA Action Plans, and external sector-led finance peer review.
findings.detail: Measures for completing the FIP and CIPFA Action Plans (target 31 March 2027), conducting an external finance peer review (target 31 December 2026), and strengthening financial management alignment (target 31 March 2027) all report 'No data' for Q1. The absence of any progress reporting is unusual for initiatives that typically require active governance oversight.
findings.matters: The existence of a mandated Financial Improvement Plan indicates prior audit concerns or financial control issues; absence of Q1 progress reporting raises questions about whether the council is actively tracking or managing its financial improvement programme.
findings.figures: Three measures (28, 29, 30) with target dates ranging from December 2026 to March 2027, all marked 'No data'

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance3_Appendix B - Q1 26-27 CSDM (Business as Usual) - All status'
findings.headline: Only 5.5% of Education, Health and Care Plans were issued within the statutory 20-week timeframe in Q1, against a 60% target.
findings.detail: The council issued 5 of 91 plans within the required timeframe. The SEND Assessment Team operates with structural capacity shortfalls: it should hold 10 FTE case officers to process the 543 annual EHCP assessment requests (currently 6 FTE) and requires 7-12 FTE annual review officers for 2,000+ active plans (currently 4 FTE). Delays are compounded by a backlog of approximately 120 educational psychology assessments and school consultation response times. EHCP numbers have grown 280% from 99 in 2020 to 376 by September 2026.
findings.matters: Systemic failure to meet statutory assessment timescales indicates the council cannot discharge a core safeguarding obligation and faces risk of intervention, complaint, legal liability, and remediation costs.
findings.figures: 5 of 91 plans (5.5%) vs 60% target; 543 EHCP requests in 2025; EHCP numbers grown from 99 (2020) to 376 (2025); 2,000+ active EHCPs; ~120 EP assessment backlog; 6 FTE case officers vs 10 required; 4 FTE annual review officers vs 7-12 required
findings.quote: According to national guidance, the number of cases EHCP officers are expected to hold over a year (i.e. assessments for new Plans and the issuing of new Plans) is 50-60. In 2025 we had 543 requests, which means the benchmark would have been 10FTE Case Officers. Last year we had 4FTE. With the additional funding we have been given for this financial year, we now have 6 FTE.

findings.matters: Revenue savings exceeding plan provides a partial offset to the pressures elsewhere in the budget and demonstrates some financial control and cost reduction delivery.

findings.paper_title: 7. Q1 2026_27 Financial Performance Report Revenue Capital - final for scrutiny and Exec
findings.headline: Transformation programme spending is running £0.8m (20%) over budget at Q1, with a £500k additional General Fund pressure dependent on planned asset disposals being realised.
findings.detail: Transformation costs were budgeted at £4.2m but Q1 outturn shows £5.0m (adverse variance +£0.8m). This spending is funded through flexible use of capital receipts from asset disposals, with a current balance of £4.5m. The paper explicitly warns that if planned disposals are not realised, a financial pressure of c.£500k against the General Fund will crystallise.
findings.matters: The council's transformation budget is dependent on achieving planned asset sales. Delays or failure to dispose would directly add to the General Fund pressure already being experienced.
findings.figures: Transformation budget £4.2m; Q1 outturn £5.0m; adverse variance +£0.8m; capital receipts balance £4.5m; contingent General Fund pressure £500k
findings.quote: Should planned disposals not be realised, a financial pressure against the General Fund of c£500k will crystalise against the General Fund based on Q1 forecasts.

findings.paper_title: 7. Q1 2026_27 Financial Performance Report Revenue Capital - final for scrutiny and Exec
findings.headline: Balance sheet resources are forecast to decline by 97% from £47.2m (2026 actual) to £1.3m by 2028, contingent on proposed government support for DSG deficits being implemented.
findings.detail: The Liability Benchmark assumes balance sheet resources reduce to just £1.3m by 2028, down from £47.2m in 2026 and £26.0m forecast for 2027. The paper notes that future government support for DSG deficits (including proposed recoupment of up to 90% of historic deficits) would strengthen these resources. Without such support, the council faces material resource depletion.
findings.matters: A balance sheet resources position dropping to £1.3m would essentially exhaust the council's financial resilience. The position is dependent on central government policy decisions outside the council's control.
findings.figures: Balance sheet resources 2026 actual £47.2m; 2027 forecast £26.0m; 2028 forecast £1.3m; decline of 97%; Liability Benchmark 2026 £304.7m → 2029 £486.0m
findings.quote: The forecast liability benchmark assumes balance sheet resources reduce to £1.3m by 2028. Any future Government support for DSG deficits, including the proposed recoupment of up to 90% of historic deficits, would strengthen balance sheet resources, reduce the Council's reliance on external borrowing and lower the projected liability benchmark.

findings.paper_title: 7. Q1 2026_27 Financial Performance Report Revenue Capital - final for scrutiny and Exec
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision is forecast to more than double from £7.1m (2026/27) to approximately £15.3m by 2032/33, with £6.7m of the 2032/33 charge attributable to EFS repayment.
findings.detail: The Q1 forecast MRP charge for 2026/27 is £7.1m, compared with £6.6m in 2025/26. Annual charges are forecast to increase to approximately £15.3m by 2032/33, of which around £6.7m relates to repayment of EFS-funded borrowing. The paper explicitly flags this rising trajectory as an important affordability consideration.
findings.matters: This demonstrates the medium-to-long-term revenue consequences of today's EFS-funded capital decisions. The council is committing to material annual debt serviceability costs over the next 6+ years, which constrains future budget flexibility.
findings.figures: 2026/27 MRP forecast £7.1m; 2025/26 actual £6.6m; 2032/33 forecast £15.3m; EFS-related portion of 2032/33 c.£6.7m
findings.quote: the annual MRP charge is forecast to increase to approximately £15.3m by 2032/33. Of this total, around £6.7m relates to the repayment of borrowing associated with Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)

findings.paper_title: 7. Q1 2026_27 Financial Performance Report Revenue Capital - final for scrutiny and Exec
findings.headline: External borrowing is forecast to increase from £306.1m (current) to £365.6m by March 2027 and further to £486m by March 2029, with the council increasingly reliant on external debt as internal resources deplete.

findings.matters: A growing debt profile combined with depletion of internal resources fundamentally changes the council's borrowing requirements and exposes it to heightened interest rate and refinancing risk.
findings.figures: Current borrowing £306.1m (£217m long-term, £89m short-term); external borrowing forecast £365.6m (31/03/2027), £486m (31/03/2029); CFR forecast £397.3m (2027), £485.5m (2029)
findings.quote: the Council is expected to fully utilise its internal cash resources over the medium term. As a result, the Council will become increasingly reliant on external borrowing to support both its capital programme and liquidity requirements

findings.paper_title: 7. Q1 2026_27 Financial Performance Report Revenue Capital - final for scrutiny and Exec
findings.headline: The council's total EFS requirement for 2026/27 is expected to exceed the provisional £30m government allocation, with the full gap potentially reaching approximately £40m.
findings.detail: MHCLG provisionally agreed £30m of Exceptional Financial Support (EFS). The Q1 revenue forecast indicates an overspend of £9.3m, which when added to budgeted EFS creates a total requirement above the £30m allocation. Any increase requires further MHCLG consideration and approval.
findings.matters: EFS is not guaranteed and requires annual application in December with notification in February. The council faces a refinancing and government funding approval risk if the actual outturn requires more than the provisional allocation.
findings.figures: Provisional EFS allocation £30m; Q1 revenue overspend +£9.3m; total EFS gap expected c.£40m
findings.quote: the Council's total EFS requirement for 2026/27 is currently expected to exceed the provisional £30m allocation. Any increase in EFS will require further consideration and approval by MHCLG

findings.paper_title: 7. Q1 2026_27 Financial Performance Report Revenue Capital - final for scrutiny and Exec
findings.headline: The Q1 outturn forecast would reduce the General Fund Reserve from just over £10m to approximately £1m, falling below the S151 Officer's recommended sustainable level.
findings.detail: The council currently holds a General Fund Reserve of just over £10m. The Q1 forecast would reduce this to c.£1m without mitigation. findings.matters: A General Fund Reserve below recommended sustainable levels signals financial vulnerability and reduces the council's ability to absorb future shocks or demand pressures.
findings.figures: Current General Fund Reserve just over £10m; Q1 forecast c.£1m; additional EFS reserves c.£4.6m; potential mitigation to c.£5.6m
findings.quote: The Q1 2026/ 27 outturn would effectively reduce the General Fund Reserve to c.£1m, taking the fund under the 151 recommended level as being financially sustainable.

findings.paper_title: 7. Q1 2026_27 Financial Performance Report Revenue Capital - final for scrutiny and Exec
findings.headline: Children's residential care placements are driving an £8.2m (88%) adverse variance through both volume growth and rate increases in a nationally constrained market.
findings.detail: The council budgeted for 24 annualised residential clients at £499k per annum. Q1 shows 36 clients at £543k per annum, with a forecast additional 5 clients (costing c.£3.0m) based on observed trend since budget setting. The residential net cost compound annual growth rate over four years is 27%. This is statutory, demand-led, and largely unavoidable.
findings.matters: This is the primary driver of the corporate £9.3m (4.4%) adverse variance. It signals ongoing structural pressure in an area where the council has limited cost control and statutory obligations.
findings.figures: +£8.2m of £9.3m total adverse variance; placements +£9.4m; residential CAGR 27% over 4 years; 24→36 annualised clients; forecast +5 more clients costing c.£3.0m
findings.quote: The cost is driven by the complexity of children's needs, and the market for placements (there is a national shortage of suitable residential placements for children with the most complex needs).

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance2_Appendix A - Q1 26-27 CSDM (High Priority) - All status'
findings.headline: Take-up of Early Learning for 2-year-olds (EL2) at 63.2% against a 76.7% target, reflecting a shift in parental choice toward the more generous Working Parent Entitlement scheme.
findings.detail: Q1 take-up 129 of 204 eligible children. Decline is not due to reduced overall early education demand but to families choosing the expanded Working Parent Entitlement (up to 30 funded hours per week available from April 2024) over the EL2 offer (which supports disadvantaged families, those on certain benefits, children with EHCP, and children in care). Council is implementing redesigned promotional materials and targeted engagement approaches to reverse the decline.
findings.matters: Funding follows take-up; lower EL2 participation affects resource allocation to early education services and the council's ability to support disadvantaged families as intended by the entitlement.
findings.figures: 63.2% take-up (Q1), target 76.7%; 129 / 204 children
findings.quote: Since April 2024, eligible working parents of 2-year-olds have been able to access a funded childcare entitlement which subsequently expanded to provide up to 30 funded hours per week for eligible working families.

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance2_Appendix A - Q1 26-27 CSDM (High Priority) - All status'
findings.headline: 16-17 year-old participation in education and training at 90.4% against a 95% target, with council now at risk of falling into the third national quintile for NEET performance for the first time.
findings.detail: Current NEET rate is circa 4% (approximately 160 young people). Council attributes structural decline to limited Level 1 and 2 education and training opportunities, reduced apprenticeship vacancies, and wider labour market pressures. A mitigating factor is the imminent transition of Newbury College into the Activate Learning Group, expected to improve local provision over time, particularly at lower qualification levels.
findings.matters: Falling youth participation in education and training indicates either deteriorating local economic conditions or inadequate capacity to meet education and training needs; either signals challenges for the council's tax base and community outcomes.

findings.quote: there is a risk of falling into the third national quintile for NEET measures for the first time.

findings.paper_title: 10. Performance2_Appendix A - Q1 26-27 CSDM (High Priority) - All status'
findings.headline: Affordable housing completions in Q1 were 24 against a target of 37, with recovery expected in later quarters but annual delivery now contingent on construction schedules outside council control.
findings.detail: Q1 delivered only 65% of target completions (24 vs 37). Council expects increases in Q2 and Q3 to reach the annual target of 146 homes, but acknowledged that this depends on when providers complete work rather than council-directed delivery.
findings.matters: Housing delivery is a measured council objective; slippage in Q1 creates execution risk against annual targets, particularly where completion timing depends on external registered providers.
findings.figures: 24 completed (Q1), target 37; annual target 146; Q1 ratio 24/37
findings.quote: The completion pipeline targets are occurring later in the year...An increase in completions is expected by the Q2 and Q3.

findings.matters: A lender evaluating debt capacity and servicing costs must track borrowing trajectory. Rapid increases in absolute debt levels, combined with depleting reserves and rising interest rate environment, signal refinancing pressure and affordability stress.

findings.detail: Balance sheet resources (cash and liquid assets available for financing) are forecast to decline from £47.2m (actual 2026) to £26.0m (2027), £1.3m (2028), and become negative at £5.6m deficit by 2029. This depletion means the council will exhaust internal cash resources and become entirely dependent on external borrowing for liquidity and capital financing. The liability benchmark is projected to exceed the CFR by 2027/28, forcing reserve drawdown followed by external borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender assesses refinancing risk and ability to meet obligations. Movement from reserves-based to debt-based funding means loss of liquidity buffer, dependence on capital markets access, and higher interest costs. Depleted reserves leave no shock absorption capacity.

findings.matters: A lender must assess refinancing risk. The council's budget is dependent on discretionary government support that exceeds allocated amounts. If EFS is not approved at required levels, the council faces a funding gap with limited mitigation beyond reserve depletion.

The National Audit Office has concluded residential care costs have almost doubled nationally in recent years.
findings.matters: Children's residential care is a statutory service with limited ability to defer or reduce. The 27% compound annual growth rate far exceeds inflation and shows no sign of moderating, creating ongoing revenue pressure that is difficult to control through discretionary savings.

findings.matters: A section 25 statement is a formal statutory warning that the council may not be able to meet its commitments. This is a direct signal to lenders that the council's finances are at serious risk of not being serviceable.

findings.detail: The paper identifies a structural income and expenditure gap requiring delivery of a Finance Improvement Plan, adopted in December 2025. A Finance Improvement Group has been established for external challenge and assurance. The paper emphasises the plan is essential for achieving financial resilience without EFS, but does not provide evidence of full delivery.
findings.matters: A structural gap by definition cannot be closed by efficiency alone; it indicates the council's service scope or funding model must change. Failure to deliver a credible plan means indefinite dependence on exceptional support.

findings.detail: The high needs deficit within the Dedicated Schools Grant was reduced by £4.8m compared to forecast. However, the statutory override that keeps DSG deficits off the general fund expires 31 March 2028. The paper explicitly states the override exists to prevent catastrophic balance-sheet failure and an s114 scenario (formal declaration that spending commitments cannot be met).
findings.matters: Once the override ends in March 2028, DSG deficits will hit the general fund balance sheet directly. Without a credible high-needs funding solution, the council faces a potential s114 notice, the most serious governance failure a council can declare.

EFS was initially forecast at £20m but reduced to £17m following Q3-Q4 improvements. However, EFS is explicitly stated as short-term assistance and must be repaid with compound interest, creating a future debt servicing burden.
findings.matters: EFS debt must be repaid with compound interest, creating a future liability that compounds the structural deficit. Reliance on EFS signals the council cannot balance its budget from revenue, raising questions about the viability of its current service model.

findings.paper_title: 5. Audit & Risk Committee - Treasury Management Review 2025-26
findings.headline: Council's short-term borrowing tactic (12-18 months) now exposed to refinancing risk as PWLB rates have risen and volatility increased

However, it now acknowledges 'increased geopolitical uncertainty and inflationary pressures due to the conflict in the Middle East have heightened interest rate risk' and will review strategy for 2026/27. PWLB 25-year rates rose from 5.8% to 6.2% in one year. Short-term loans represent £74.2m, or 24% of total borrowing, requiring refinancing within one year.
findings.matters: A tactical bet on falling rates is now exposed to refinancing £74m of debt into a higher-rate environment, increasing debt service costs at a time of budget stress

It requires 'long term borrowing to fund capital and liquidity' with 'rare' occurrence indicating 'immediate need' for external borrowing.
findings.matters: This is an extreme financial position indicating the council must borrow for liquidity. It creates severe interest rate and refinancing risk and signals potential inability to fund capital programmes or manage emergencies.

findings.paper_title: 4. Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 -2030 public
findings.headline: Council will have no internal investable resources left from 2027/28 onwards; Liability Benchmark exceeds CFR and council becomes fully exposed to interest rate risk
findings.detail: The council's reserves and cash balances will be fully depleted by 2027/28 when the Liability Benchmark exceeds the Capital Financing Requirement. From that point, all borrowing will be at market rates with no buffer from internal resources. Simultaneously, capital financing costs are projected to grow £14.8m over the MTFS (from £15.6m to £30.92m), driven by EFS financing and rising interest costs.
findings.matters: Total depletion of reserves removes financial flexibility and crisis buffers; full exposure to interest rate movements creates unhedgeable risk; rising financing costs as a percentage of revenue (8.5% to 15.9% of net revenue stream) signals unsustainable debt trajectory

findings.quote: Based on current projections in the MTFS, and the EFS requirement to support the reserves and net revenue budget in 2026/27, the Liability Benchmark will exceed the CFR in financial year 2027/28. This effectively means the internal investable resources (reserves, cash balances), have been fully depleted from an internal financing perspective and the Authority is fully exposed to interest rate risk.

findings.paper_title: 4. Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 -2030 public
findings.headline: Council tax base reduced by 854 dwellings and collection rate cut from 99.5% to 98.6%, creating permanent £12.5m revenue loss
findings.detail: The council has revised down its tax base assumptions after reviewing actual dwelling numbers and collection patterns. Slower housebuilding (attributed to sustained high interest rates) and increased demand for council tax support and reliefs have combined to reduce the tax base. This adjustment permanently reduces the council's own-resource funding capacity and reduces settlement-based CSP growth from £19.8m to £14.9m.
findings.matters: A shrinking tax base signals local economic difficulty and reduces the council's borrowing capacity (which is often based on tax base multiples); it indicates a structural, not cyclical, revenue weakness
findings.figures: Reduction of 854 equivalent dwellings; collection rate reduced from 99.5% to 98.6%; cumulative revenue reduction £12.5m over MTFS period; reduces CSP growth from £19.8m to £14.9m
findings.quote: The Council's collection rate, historically set at +99%, has been adjusted to 98.60%. The number of taxable dwelling has been reduced by 854. The reduction in growth compared to projections is largely attributable to the wider economic environment, with the building of anticipated developments slowing in a prolonged period of high interest rates. The cost-of-living crisis has also resulted in the number of households seeking support and reliefs to grow during the reporting period.

findings.paper_title: 4. Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 -2030 public

findings.detail: Social care is described as the primary driver of the £53.3m net revenue budget growth. Unit costs are escalating due to both complexity of need and market factors (national living wage, employer NI). The top 25 individual care packages alone cost £13.1m in 2025/26 compared to £4.9m in 2019/20 — a 168% cost inflation in four years. The council requires £33.7m net investment in commissioning budgets across the MTFS.
findings.matters: Social care is demand-led and largely fixed in the short term; rising unit costs show no signs of stabilisation; this expenditure pressure is outpacing all other council services and cannot be easily controlled through efficiency savings
findings.figures: Social care commissioning growth +£39.4m net; top 25 care packages £13.1m (2025/26) vs £4.9m (2019/20); £33.7m net investment required over MTFS

In financial year 2025/26, the total annual cost of care packages for the top twenty-five packages amounted to £13.1 million, compared to £4.9 million in 2019/20.

Thereafter annual requirements climb steeply: £30m (2026/27), £40m (2027/28), £47m (2028/29-2029/30). By 2028/29, EFS accounts for over 100% of the council's capital financing requirement movement, meaning the entire borrowing need is being funded by revenue capitalisation.
findings.matters: Escalating EFS requests signal that structural budget pressures are worsening rather than stabilising; EFS is unsustainable medium-term and dependent on continued government forbearance; it also drives up Minimum Revenue Provision costs in future years
findings.quote: However, a challenging 2025/26 in year financial position, has presented a significant pressure against the Council's minimal General Fund, resulting in a revised 2025/26 £20 million EFS request as detailed below... The Council is in receipt of financial support from Central Government (2024/25 £13 million, and 2025/26 provisionally agreed £3 million, with revised request for £20 million submitted).

findings.paper_title: 4. Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 -2030 public
findings.headline: Council cannot balance 2026/27 budget without further central government support; faces Section 114 notice if denied
findings.detail: After completing savings identification exercises, the council explicitly states it cannot set a balanced 2026/27 budget without additional EFS. The s151 officer is required to issue a Section 114 notice if this support is not approved or alternative major efficiencies are not presented. This pattern repeats annually throughout the MTFS period.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a formal statement of financial distress that triggers statutory intervention; it signals the council cannot meet its statutory duty to balance the budget and represents a material governance failure
findings.quote: Following the conclusion of savings identification exercises, the Council is unable to set a balanced budget for financial year 2026/27 without seeking additional financial support from Central Government. A request for such financial support was submitted on 12th December 2025. Without approval of this support, or alternatively a robust plan of efficiencies (of such scale, well beyond those of prior financial years), provided for review to the Executive, the s151 officer will be required to issue a Section 114 report/notice. This pattern is repeated annually throughout the MTFS.

findings.detail: The ratio of capital financing costs to net revenue stream breaches the council's adopted 10% maximum in 2027/28 (reaching 12.1%) and continues rising to 15.9% by 2029/30. This means debt servicing is consuming an ever-larger share of available revenue.
findings.matters: Unsustainable financing ratios reduce capacity for service investment and indicate deteriorating financial sustainability as debt costs dominate budget flexibility.
findings.quote: The adopted ratio above, although compliant in 2026/27, is exceeded in 2027/28

findings.paper_title: 5. Treasury Management Strategy - Investment Borrowing 2026-27
findings.headline: Council moves into negative working capital from 2025/26, driven by borrowing and High Needs Block deficit
findings.detail: Working capital (current assets minus current liabilities) turns negative from 2025/26 onwards, indicating the council owes more in the short term than it has in liquid resources. This is driven by increasing borrowing liabilities and growing High Needs Block deficits.
findings.matters: Negative working capital signals potential liquidity stress and suggests difficulty managing short-term obligations without further borrowing or asset sales.
findings.quote: From 2025/26 the Authority moves to a negative working capital position, this is primarily driven by increasing current liabilities relating to borrowing, and revenue pressures alongside the increasing High Needs Block deficit

findings.paper_title: 5. Treasury Management Strategy - Investment Borrowing 2026-27
findings.headline: General Fund reserves collapse from £15.83m to £0.52m over four years
findings.detail: The General Fund falls from £15.83m in 2025/26 to £12.17m (2026/27), £8.02m (2027/28), and just £0.52m by 2028/29—essentially zero. This eliminates the council's ability to absorb unforeseen costs or variations in income.
findings.matters: Minimal reserves mean the council cannot manage volatility in demand, inflation, or income without service reductions or further borrowing.
findings.quote: the Authority's investable resources are being depleted over the life of the MTFS, with usable reserves (even after application of EFS), are reducing

findings.paper_title: 5. Treasury Management Strategy - Investment Borrowing 2026-27
findings.headline: Internal reserves will be fully exhausted by 2027/28, forcing full exposure to interest rate risk
findings.detail: The Liability Benchmark will exceed the Capital Financing Requirement in 2027/28, meaning the council will have depleted all internal cash resources. Once reserves are gone, the council must borrow for all future needs and has no buffer against interest rate movements.
findings.matters: Complete depletion of internal resources eliminates financial flexibility and forces the council into perpetual external borrowing with no shock absorption capacity.
findings.quote: the Liability Benchmark will exceed the CFR in financial year 2027/28. This effectively means the internal investable resources (reserves, cash balances), have been fully depleted from an internal financing perspective and the Authority is fully exposed to interest rate risk

findings.paper_title: 5. Treasury Management Strategy - Investment Borrowing 2026-27
findings.headline: Council's own treasury assessment concludes it is experiencing 'financial distress'
findings.detail: The council's finance team explicitly describes its position as showing 'a level of financial distress', with future financing driven by EFS requests rather than capital programmes. This language from management signals awareness of structural problems beyond cyclical pressures.
findings.matters: When a council's own finance officers describe the position as financially distressed, it indicates serious creditworthiness concerns and reduced repayment capacity.
findings.figures: Financing costs as % of net revenue: 10.0% (2026/27), 12.1% (2027/28), 14.3% (2028/29), vs 10% adopted maximum
findings.quote: The financing ratio, alongside the liability benchmark demonstrates a level of financial distress, with treasury indicators highlighting financing requirements in financial years, subsequent to 2026/27, being heavily influenced by EFS requests as opposed to purely financing historic and proposed capital programmes

findings.paper_title: 5. Treasury Management Strategy - Investment Borrowing 2026-27
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) becomes the primary driver of borrowing need, not capital spending
findings.detail: The council's underlying borrowing requirement (CFR) is increasingly driven by capitalisation of revenue overspends rather than actual capital investment. EFS requests are rising from £30m in 2026/27 to £47m by 2028/29, and by 2028/29, 100% of CFR growth will be EFS-driven. This indicates the council cannot balance its revenue budget without government support.
findings.matters: Dependence on discretionary EFS rather than self-sufficiency signals structural budget imbalance and reliance on government support that may not continue indefinitely.
findings.quote: by the end of the MTFS, 100% of the movement in CFR will be driven by EFS

findings.paper_title: 6.1 Capital Strategy Covering Report 2026-2030
findings.headline: MTFS projects a significant funding gap in 2026/27, with revenue capital financing requirements as a contributing factor
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy shows a material funding gap in the coming financial year. The gap is partly driven by revenue capital financing costs (debt servicing for the capital strategy), indicating that revenue pressures and capital financing costs are both squeezing the budget.
findings.matters: A funding gap signals the council must make additional savings, raise income, or draw down reserves; gaps that persist suggest structural deficit
findings.figures: Funding gap amount not specified but described as 'significant'
findings.quote: The proposed MTFS details a significant funding gap for financial year 2026/27. An element of the gap is being driven by the revenue capital financing requirement (debt servicing), incurred supporting delivery of the Council's Capital Strategy and the associated programme of works.

findings.paper_title: 6.1 Capital Strategy Covering Report 2026-2030
findings.headline: PWLB borrowing rates at 5.5% against historic 2-3% average, significantly raising financing costs
findings.detail: High interest rates substantially increase the cost of capital financing, compressing the revenue budget further and reducing the affordability of the capital programme. This is a key constraint on the council's ability to deliver investment.
findings.matters: Higher debt servicing costs reduce available revenue for services and capital investment; further rate rises would worsen the funding gap
findings.figures: 5.5% current PWLB rates vs historic 2-3% average
findings.quote: The Council's ability to deliver a capital programme has been constrained by two key factors: Firstly, by a high-interest rate environment, Public Works and Loan Board (PWLB) rates on average being around 5.5% compared to a historic 2 -3% average.

findings.paper_title: 6.1 Capital Strategy Covering Report 2026-2030
findings.headline: Council-funded capital programme significantly reduced; shift to external grants as internal resources are depleted
findings.detail: Capital investment capacity is being squeezed as EFS requirements and HNB deficit consume Balance Sheet resources. The council is actively refocusing the capital programme onto only key projects and moving toward reliance on external grants and contributions rather than council borrowing.
findings.matters: Reduced capital investment signals constraints on infrastructure maintenance and service improvement; long-term asset condition and service delivery may deteriorate
findings.figures: £49 million council-funded capital vs £165 million EFS need over MTFS
findings.quote: The Council-funded (i.e. debt funded) capital programme over the life of the MTFS (2026/27 -2029/30) has been significantly reduced compared to prior financial years. The reduction has been driven by a significant increase in the Council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR), through an increasing need to seek Exceptional Financial Support (EFS).

findings.paper_title: 6.1 Capital Strategy Covering Report 2026-2030
findings.headline: High Needs Block deficit growing from £30.5m to £51.7m, eroding usable reserves and forcing external borrowing
findings.detail: The DSG-related HNB deficit is forecast to grow substantially and is being held in unusable reserves under statutory override until 31 March 2028. This is reducing working capital and forcing the council to borrow externally to support both capital and capitalised revenue expenditure.
findings.matters: A structural overspend in education demand is forcing external borrowing; the statutory override ends in 2028, at which point the deficit could impact the General Fund directly
findings.figures: £30.5 million by 31st March 2026, increasing to an estimated £51.7 million by 31st March 2027
findings.quote: The HNB deficit (related to the DSG), which is currently subject to a statutory override, (i.e. the deficit is held within the Council's Balance Sheet in unusable reserves as opposed to impacting the Council's General Fund), is forecast to be in the region of £30.5 million by 31st March 2026, increasing to an estimated £51.7 million by 31st March 2027.

findings.paper_title: 6.1 Capital Strategy Covering Report 2026-2030
findings.headline: Council forecasts over £165 million in Exceptional Financial Support needs over the MTFS period
findings.detail: EFS represents capitalised revenue overspends that must be financed through Minimum Revenue Provision charges back to the revenue budget. Against this, the council plans only £49 million in council-funded capital expenditure, meaning revenue account problems are consuming capital financing capacity.
findings.matters: EFS is a symptom of structural revenue deficit; it signals financial distress and requires government intervention, while consuming revenue that would otherwise fund services or investment
findings.figures: over £165million EFS need vs £49million planned council-funded capital expenditure
findings.quote: During the life of the Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS), there is a current projected need for EFS of over £165million compared to planned Council-funded capital expenditure of £49million.
